#5452. October 25, 2019

And it’s Friday! [Throws frisbee into tree.]

Before we dive into the newsletter, one more bit of great news about our upcoming event (which we promise we’ll stop talking about soon): Michael Grimes, the star tech banker from Morgan Stanley at the center of Uber’s IPO (and Facebook IPO, and Slack’s and Spotify’s), has been persuaded to come and talk about direct listings, which we’re very excited about. If you’re as confused as we are about whether these make sense for more than a couple of companies each year (current status: we don’t think they do), you won’t want to miss this rare conversation with “Wall Street’s Silicon Valley whisperer.”

Note that seats are almost gone. Giant thanks to NextWorld, the early-stage enterprise-focused firm that’s hosting all of us; to KCPR, the boutique tech PR and strategy firm; and to Carta, a platform that helps companies and VCs manage their cap tables, valuations, investments, and equity plans, for their support.

Ben Horowitz,  the co-founder of the venture firm Andreessen Horowitz, has a new book coming out this coming Monday titled “What You Do is Who You Are,” that takes a look at how to create “culture” at a company.

It’s a word that’s thrown around a lot but that’s very hard to grasp, let alone implement in a sustainable way. Horowitz learned firsthand as a CEO how elusive it can be when he took stock of his company, only to discover it was made up of “screamers who intimidated their people,” others who “neglected to give any feedback,” and at least one compulsive liar who excelled at sucking up to Horowitz and also making up stories from whole cloth.

Horowitz says creating culture was a missing part of his education, and in this new book — a follow-up to his best-selling “The Hard Thing About Hard Things” — he does his best to fill that gap for other CEOs, using his own experience, as well as lessons gleaned from historical figures Toussaint Louverture and Genghis Khan, along with Shaka Senghor, a contemporary who served time for murder and today is a criminal justice reform advocate.

It’s an instructive and novel combination, and we suggest picking up the book, especially if you love history. In the meantime, we sat down recently with Horowitz to talk about its timing and whether some of the biggest cultural blow-ups in the startup industry — Uber and WeWork — could have been avoided. These excerpts have been edited for length and clarity. Note that we’ll have more of the conversation — including Horowitz’s thoughts about dual-class shares —  for readers of Extra Crunch on Monday.

You’ve just written a book about culture that’s coming out just as a lot of questions are being raised about culture because of WeWork. What happened there?

[Cofounder Adam Neumann] had a certain kind of culture there. He had some holes — some great strengths and great holes. And sometimes that happens. When you’re really good at part of it, you can delude yourself into thinking that you’ve got everything you need when you have some massive incompleteness.

Adam is so amazing. Like, the way they got all the money and everything. And the vision was so spectacular. And everybody there believed it, and they recruited some phenomenal talent. But when you’re that optimistic, it does help to have something in the culture that says [allows] people to bring you the bad news, like, if the accounting is all over the place or what have you.

As with Uber’s Travis Kalanick, whose culture also came under fire, Neumann operated in very plain sight. He wasn’t hiding who he was or what he was spending.

Right, everybody knew how Travis was running the company. Everyone in Silicon Valley knew, let alone everyone on the board. The culture was published. You can look up Uber’s values [from that period].

Travis designed, I think, a really compelling culture, and believed in it, and published it. And the consequences of what he was missing were also super well-known. It’s only when board members think people are coming after them that [they take an interest in these things].

What are the biggest lessons in these two cases?

I obviously know more about Uber [as a Lyft investor who follows the space]. In Uber’s case, it’s a very subtle thing. Travis had a really good code. But he had a bug in it.

I think it was reported that, like, Travis encouraged bad behavior. I don’t think he did at all. I just think he didn’t make it clear that legal and ethical [considerations] were more important than competitiveness. As a result, when left to their own devices, in a distributed organization where there was a lot of distributed power, that combination had people doing things that were out of bounds.

And he was making everybody so much money. And the company was growing so fast that, for the board members, I suspect they were like, ‘As long as it’s making money, I’m not going to worry about what happens next.’

To me, the unfair part is, like, they shouldn’t get any credit at the end. Whatever you’re blaming Travis for [you should blame them, too] because they didn’t see it, either. I think that’s a charitable way of putting it.

#5451. Crypto and Midterm Election: 3 Risks From Trump’s $5,000 Stimulus to Iran

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Crypto is facing a major political test as Americans head to the polls on November 3, with the US midterm election potentially reshaping regulation, stimulus expectations, and investor risk appetite.

Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress, while Democrats are seeking to regain power in at least one chamber. The outcome could determine if President Donald Trump advances his economic agenda or faces a tougher legislative road ahead.

For crypto, the midterm election comes with three major risks: Trump’s proposed $5,000 stimulus dividend, the future of stalled crypto legislation, and escalating tensions with Iran.

The election itself may not immediately change Crypto’s fundamentals. However, it could shift expectations around liquidity, regulation, and the financial markets.

Trump has promised a $5,000 dividend payment to adult US citizens if Republicans retain control of both the House and Senate. The proposal would cover 240 million adults, potentially costing around $1.2 trillion, and Trump has also suggested that tariff revenue could help fund the payments.

Trump may have just sealed the deal on stage in Dallas.He's promising a $5,000 dividend to every American adult if Republicans win the midterms — only condition is the money has to be spent in the U.S.I've never seen anything like this. pic.twitter.com/ypJP2fYsLj

A Republican victory could then strengthen expectations for additional household spending and potentially inject fresh liquidity into financial markets. We, in the crypto market, have historical reasons to watch stimulus closely.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, US stimulus checks coincided with extraordinary monetary easing and a powerful crypto rally. A Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland study found that the 2020 payments increased Bitcoin buy volume by 3.8%, while the associated price effect was modest.

The 2020–2021 rally also benefited from low interest rates, institutional adoption, and abundant liquidity. Hence, a new stimulus program could encourage retail investors to allocate more money toward Bitcoin and other risk assets.

However, the proposed dividend is not approved, and higher inflation expectations or Treasury yields could offset some of the bullish impact. If Democrats win control of Congress, Trump’s proposal could face a much tougher path toward approval.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

The Midterm election could also determine whether lawmakers make progress on the most-awaited crypto regulation, the Digital Asset Market CLARITY Act. It aims to establish clearer rules governing digital assets and the division of responsibilities between US regulators.

The bill remains stalled after failing to advance through a Senate procedural vote in September. A Republican victory could improve its chances, although bipartisan support would still be necessary to overcome legislative hurdles.

A Democratic victory, particularly if the party takes control of the House, could bring increased scrutiny of Trump’s crypto-related ventures and campaign connections. That could delay legislation as lawmakers focus on investigations and oversight.

Still, a Democratic win would not automatically mean tougher crypto regulation. Bipartisan support for clearer digital asset rules remains possible, although the final legislation could look different from the current proposal.

The Midterm election presents a mixed outlook for crypto. A Republican victory combined with stimulus optimism, progress on crypto legislation, and Iran de-escalation would create a potentially bullish environment.

A Democratic victory could introduce regulatory uncertainty, while renewed conflict in the Middle East could pressure crypto regardless of the midterm election result. For us, the key question is whether political optimism can outweigh geopolitical risk.

Trump’s stimulus promise may offer a powerful bullish narrative, but crypto’s next major move could ultimately depend on improving liquidity or another inflationary shock.

The biggest immediate threat to crypto is not the midterm election, and it may come from outside Washington. The US carried out limited strikes on Iran’s Qeshm islands near the Strait of Hormuz. This revived concerns about escalation, even as diplomatic contacts continued.

The Glamsterdam upgrade on Hoodi, previously scheduled for October 26, 2026 at 17:42:48 UTC (epoch 132,352), was postponed and a new activation date has not been set.

Core developers decided on ACDE #248 to delay the previously scheduled Glamsterdam network upgrade on the Hoodi testnet to allow for further investigation of interactions of EIP-8037 with mainnet smart contracts.

The delay removes the scheduled Amsterdam execution layer activation and Gloas consensus layer activation. It also removes the gas-limit schedule that would have raised Hoodi's gas limit to 200 million at the same epoch. A revised Hoodi activation schedule is expected to be announced separately.

#5449. October 28, 2019

Revolution, the investment firm cofounded 14 years ago by entrepreneur-investor Steve Case, has closed its second Rise of the Rest seed fund with $150 million in capital commitments, just like the debut fund it announced two years ago.

Rise of the Rest — which fund startups outside of the biggest U.S. tech hubs in an effort to foster innovation and momentum elsewhere — has rounded up some of the funding from institutional investors, presumably, but also from numerous very wealthy individuals.

According to Forbes, which is currently hosting a summit where Case announced the new fund, some of the new fund’s backers include Jeff Bezos of Amazon, Sara Blakely of Spanx, hedge fund manager Ray Dalio, Under Armour cofounder Kevin Plank, former Tennessee governor Bill Haslam, and Apollo Global Management cofounder Joshua Harris.

Some of these investors backed the first fund, too, including Bezos and Dalio.

Very notably, Hillbilly Elegy author J.D. Vance, who ran the first fund with Case, has stepped back, and longtime Revolution investor David Hall will manage the second fund instead.

Certainly, that first fund kept its investors busy, with stakes in 125 companies. Barely a week passes without a startup announcing some funding from the Rise of the Rest team.

ACV Auctions, a five-year-old, Buffalo, N.Y.-based online platform for franchise and used-car dealerships to buy and sell wholesale inventory through 20-minute auctions, is reportedly looking to raise $150 million in Series E funding at a post-money valuation north of $1 billion. Reuters has more here.

Weave, a seven-year-old, Lehi, Ut.-based developer of patient communications software focused on the dental and optometry market, has raised $70 million in Series D funding at a post-money valuation of $970 million. Tiger Global Management led the round, with participation from earlier backers Catalyst Investors, Bessemer Venture Partners, Crosslink Capital, Pelion Venture Partners and LeadEdge Capital. TechCrunch has more here.

1906, a two-year-old, Denver-based cannabis brand that makes a wide variety of edibles, has raised $18 million in funding led by Navy Capital. More here.

Choco, an 18-month-old, mobile ordering platform for restaurants and their suppliers, has raised $33.5 million in Series A funding by Bessemer Venture Partners. The company has now raised $41 million to date. Other investors include Atlantic Labs, Target Global, Visionaries Club and Greyhound. TechCrunch has more here.

Duffel, a two-year-old, London-based startup that connects travel agencies with airline reservation systems, has raised $30 million in Series B funding led by Index Ventures, with participation from earlier backers Benchmark and Blossom Capital. TechCrunch has more here.

Sensely, a five-year-old, San Francisco-based chatbot that helps users navigate insurance benefits, has raised $15 million led by Aflac Corporate Ventures, with participation from NMC, Nippon Life Insurance Company, Susquehanna International Group, Sojitz Corporation, Zuelling Pharma and Silicon Valley Bank. MobiHealth News has more here.

ShiraTronics, a 10-month-old, Brooklyn Park, Mn.-based medical device company working on a migraine treatment, raised $33 million in Series A funding. USVP, Amzak Health and Strategic HealthCare Investment Partners led the round, joined by Aperture Ventures and LivaNova. Welcome to the Jungle, a five-year-old, Paris-based recruitment startup, has raised $22.3 million in fresh funding led by Gaia Capital Partners, with participation from Bpifance, XAnge, and Jean-Paul Guisset. TechCrunch has more here.

EnsureDR, a five-year-old, San Jose, Ca.-based company that makes disaster recovery readiness software, has raised $2.5 million in Series A funding led by Awz Ventures. More here.

Own Up, a 3.5-year-old, Boston-based startup that invites promises users a high-touch service if they connect with its team of online mortgage brokers, has raised $8.5 million in Series A funding. Link Ventures led the round. More here.

#5448. Vitalik Devcon Cosplay Steals the Show as Bitmine Loads Up on More Ethereum

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Devcon attendees got an unexpected laugh when Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin appeared on stage wearing a green cloak and a smiling mask. The unusual cosplay stole the spotlight as Bitmine ETH accumulation continued, with the company adding another 8,573 Ethereum to its massive treasury.

Buterin’s costume looked more suited to a fantasy game than one of crypto’s biggest developer gatherings. The playful Vitalik appearance offered a lighter moment at Devcon 8 in Mumbai, where developers and researchers are discussing Ethereum’s future.

Meanwhile, Bitmine Immersion Technologies is pursuing a much more serious mission: accumulating enough ETH to control 5% of its total supply. The company’s latest disclosure showed holdings of 6,060,506 ETH as of November 1, worth $13.7 billion at its current price of $2,261. Bitmine now controls around 4.9% of Ethereum’s supply, putting it close to its ambitious accumulation target.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Devcon 8 runs from November 3 to November 6 in Mumbai, bringing Ethereum developers, researchers, and ecosystem participants together for four days of talks and workshops. But Buterin’s unusual outfit delivered an unexpected highlight during the event.

The Vitalik Devcon appearance showed the lighter side of Ethereum’s culture, even as the network faces serious questions about adoption, scaling, and ETH’s market performance.

@VitalikButerin just opened Devcon and set the tone for the week.A formally verified OS, open silicon, self-sovereign healthtech, free discourse, private communication, trustworthy AI — these are all part of Ethereum's mission. https://t.co/51UfMsxk5o pic.twitter.com/TynzSuzmhX

Bitmine, however, appears unfazed by the market uncertainty. The company purchased 8,573 ETH during the latest reported week, worth roughly $19.4 million at its disclosed valuation. Its total crypto, cash, and other investments reached $14.5 billion, including 216 BTC and $498 million in cash and marketable securities.

🧵1/BitMine provided its latest holdings update for November 2, 2026$14.5 billion in total crypto + "moonshots":– 6,060,506 ETH at $2,261per ETH (per @coinbase)– 216 Bitcoin (BTC)– $180 million stake in Beast Industries @MrBeast– $82 million stake in Eightco Holdings…

Bitmine has also staked 5.23 million ETH, representing 86% of its holdings. The company estimates that its current staking position could generate around $358 million in annualized rewards, potentially rising to $415 million if its entire ETH treasury were staked.

That creates a second part of its Ethereum thesis. Accumulating the asset while generating yield from the network.

Ethereum’s bullish outlook rests on more than Bitmine’s buying activity. Staking removes ETH from immediate trading circulation, while institutional treasury accumulation can add another source of demand. Bitmine’s holdings alone now represent nearly one in every 20 ETH in existence.

The company’s growing staking position also shows Ethereum’s proof-of-stake model, where holders can earn rewards by helping secure the network. Bitmine’s projected staking income gives it an incentive to maintain its ETH exposure rather than simply trade around short-term price moves.

Price forecasts remain ambitious. Bitmine Chairman Tom Lee has suggested Ethereum could revisit its previous all-time high near $4,954 before the end of 2026, with $6,000 also emerging as a potential year-end target.

At $2,261, ETH would need to climb 119% to reach $4,954 and around 165% to hit $6,000. The technical picture still needs improvement. Ethereum faces resistance around the $2,315 area, identified as a key moving-average level in recent market analysis.

A sustained move above that zone could strengthen the recovery case, while a failure to reclaim it would leave ETH vulnerable to further downside.

There are risks to the bullish thesis. U.S. spot Ethereum ETFs recorded substantial outflows during October, while ETH’s price performance remained under pressure. Institutional accumulation has not yet translated into a decisive market reversal.

Still, Bitmine’s continued buying, its massive staked position, and Ethereum’s potential price recovery are keeping long-term bulls engaged.

Vitalik and his Devcon cosplay may have provided the conference’s funniest moment, but Bitmine’s growing treasury is the more serious signal. If institutional demand returns and ETH breaks through key resistance, $6,000 could move back into the conversation.

#5447. Series B Funding Is Up, But Fewer Deals Are Getting Done

More money, fewer rounds. That, in short, is the state of U.S. Series B startup funding in 2026, as venture capital investment continues to concentrate heavily around a handful of AI hotshots.

Crunchbase data shows that so far this year, investors have poured around $48 billion into financings around the Series B stage 1, the highest tally in years. Yet round counts are below year-ago levels and are on track for a multiyear low.

One trend driving capital concentration is a sharp decline in small and mid-sized Series B rounds.

So far this year, less than a third of deals in our sample set 2 were for under $30 million. By contrast, between 2021 and 2025, rounds in this range accounted for about half of deals, per Crunchbase data.

The smallest Series B deals have gotten particularly scarce. This year there were just 26 rounds under $10 million in our sample set.

On the flip side, really large Series B rounds are quite popular.

At least 110 companies have raised rounds of $100 million or more around this stage so far this year. That’s roughly a quarter of all deals.

Of these, the largest by far was a $12 billion round 3 for Prometheus, Jeff Bezos’ physical AI startup that launched last year.

Model developer World Labs, led by AI pioneer Fei-Fei Li, was tied for next-biggest fundraiser, closing on $1 billion in February. Nuclear energy startup Valar Atomics also secured $1 billion in Series B funding across tranches this year, with Sequoia Capital as lead investor.

For  a wider snapshot, below we put together a sample list of more of this year’s biggest U.S. Series B recipients.

Meanwhile, one of the least surprising findings from our analysis of Series B recipients is that it was a heavily AI-focused group.

So far this year, about two-thirds of Series B funding has gone to AI-focused startups, per Crunchbase data. In 2025, by comparison, about half of investment went to companies in AI categories.

AI companies were also heavily represented by round count. So far in 2026, more than half of all reported U.S. Series B deals have been for AI companies.

Overall, the numbers point to a bullish climate for Series B investment, particularly for AI startups with demonstrated traction. The environment looks particularly favorable for companies that have already raised considerable sums at Series A and seed.

Even so, these don’t look like the best of times for startups seeking smaller Series B rounds. Seems like in the current AI-driven cycle, investors are increasingly focused on big checks for high-valuation companies.

May include rounds that have characteristics of Series B financings but were not explicitly announced as Series B deals.↩

Sample included U.S. Series B rounds of $1 million or more.↩

Prometheus did not publicly announce its $12 billion funding round as a Series B, but reports from multiple sources, including an Axios post, described it as Series B.↩

#5446. October 29, 2019

Chan Park feels like “an eternal nomad.” He has since age 12, when he moved from Korea to the U.S., where he attended middle school in Minnesota, followed by high school in New Jersey, followed by college in New Hampshire. Then he really began to bounce around. Park worked as a trader in New York out of college, embraced the ski-bum life in Utah, then headed to Asia for Uber, where he spent six years, running its expansion team, then managing its entire Southeast Asia business out of Singapore.

More specifically, he was responsible for eight countries across the region, and 350 people, which didn’t give him a lot of time to organize his home. But he wasn’t overwhelmed by the chaos. Instead, he says that in Singapore, something unusual happened. “There’s this huge culture of landlords furnishing space to attract expats,” explains Park. “The furnishings aren’t super high-end, but they’re well-designed and well put together, and it enabled me to be basically moved in as soon as I put my clothes in the closet.” Suddenly, coming home was a treat — a new sensation for him. “For the first time, I was proud to host friends for dinners and barbecues and to just open the door and relax.”

Park knew his U.S. friends could benefit from the same experience, and before long, he was talking with his Dartmouth classmate turned product and industrial designer Christian Talmage about forming their own company. Enter Oliver Space, which provides a lot of what that Singaporean landlord delivered to Park. It furnishes places for busy professionals, making moving into a new home as easy as hanging up their clothes.

The now year-old service is available in the Bay Area only. And Oliver Space employs just a dozen people so far. But the company has already gained enough traction to attract $6.8 million in seed funding from an interesting array of investors, including Mayfield, Abstract Ventures, investors Jana Messerschmidt and April Underwood, Opendoor founder Eric Wu, and Kevin and Julia Hartz of Eventbrite, among others.

Now, Oliver Space just has to grow as quickly, or more so, than other furniture-as-service startups to recently attract funding.

Dogecoin traders faced fresh pressure amid the ongoing market drop, with 17,833,333 DOGE in long positions liquidated as selling returned to the market. $342 million was liquidated across the crypto market in the last 24 hours, with Dogecoin having its share.

According to CoinGlass data, Dogecoin saw a total of $2.45 million in liquidations over the last 24 hours, with longs accounting for $1.391 million (about 17,833,333 DOGE) of this total, while shorts saw $1.05 million in liquidations.

Long liquidations occur when traders betting on higher prices are forced to close their positions, typically after losses push their margin balances below required levels. When large numbers of leveraged positions are liquidated in a short period, the resulting selling can intensify downward price pressure.

Along these lines, Dogecoin was down nearly 3% in the last 24 hours to $0.078 as the market fell while investors digested the Federal Reserve's decision to hold interest rates steady at its October meeting.

Dogecoin rose for three consecutive days earlier in the week to hit $0.08, but profit-taking in the markets caused its price to retreat.

The Personal Consumption Expenditures Index—the Fed's preferred inflation gauge—was released Thursday, with few cryptocurrencies recouping losses in the wake of the report.

The personal consumption expenditures price index increased a seasonally adjusted 0.5% for the month, putting the annual inflation rate at 3.6% as the pace of price increases stepped up in September, keeping inflation well above the Federal Reserve's target.

While the Fed held interest rates on Wednesday, as expected, two officials dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase and Chair Kevin Warsh declined to signal what might come in December. However, expectations for a 25 basis point hike at the central bank's next meeting on Dec. 9 remain.

If Dogecoin rebounds, the next key resistance levels for Dogecoin are $0.083 and $0.087, while support is envisaged first at $0.074 and $0.069 in the event of a price drop.

#5444. Sector Snapshot: Travel Tech Funding Heads Toward Multiyear Low Despite AI Push

Travel demand appears to be holding up, but at the same time, investor appetite for travel tech startups has cooled. Even a wave of startups promising to improve travel with AI hasn’t managed to reverse the funding slowdown, a review of Crunchbase data shows. Whether uncertainty over how AI will reshape travel planning and booking is contributing to that pullback remains an open question.

Startups in the travel tech space have raised $2.2 billion this year through the third quarter, according to Crunchbase data. The largest funding recipients span a wide range of categories including hotel management software, travel booking platforms, alternative accommodations and corporate events. The mix also includes electric aviation, travel finance and insurance, and consumer hospitality businesses, reflecting a broad definition of travel tech.

The broad trend: Investors are making far fewer bets on travel startups than immediately before and after the COVID-19 pandemic, Crunchbase data shows. This year could be the lowest since at least 2018 when it comes to dollars raised and deal count.

AI is a recurring theme among the largest funding recipients, with many using it to perform functions such as automating hospitality operations, personalizing bookings and streamlining travel planning.

The numbers: In the first three quarters of 2026, startups in the travel tech space have raised $2.2 billion globally across just 302 funding rounds, Crunchbase data shows. That’s down fairly significantly so far from the $3.7 billion raised in 2025. Deal volume is on track to fall for a third consecutive year — pointing to a market where investors are putting more money into fewer companies.

Funding and deal volume in recent years remain far below past levels. In 2021, for example, funding in the sector topped $12 billion. That’s a bit surprising considering that so much travel was halted in the midst of the COVID-19 pandemic. But even prior to the pandemic, funding and deal totals were much higher — totaling $9.4 billion across 1,277 deals in 2018 and $10.4 billion across 1,190 transactions in 2019.

Even travel industry researcher Skift noted the funding downturn in a recent newsletter, saying: “Though it’s too early to say whether this is a long-term market movement, it’s a clear sign of the times.”

Interestingly, several of the year’s largest deals involved startups headquartered outside of the United States.

The year’s largest funding recipient through the third quarter was Mews, which raised a $300 million Series D in January led by EQT Growth, with participation from Atomico, HarbourVest Partners, Kinnevik, Battery Ventures and Tiger Global Management. The Amsterdam-based hospitality software company helps hotels manage reservations, payments and operations, and says it plans to expand its use of AI agents to automate workflows. The financing valued the company at $2.5 billion.

Chinese electric aircraft developer Aerofugia raised about $144 million in February in a financing led by CITIC Securities, joined by New Alliance Capital, Vertex Ventures China and other investors. Chengdu-based Aerofugia, also backed by automaker Geely, develops electric passenger aircraft that take off and land vertically, often called flying taxis.

Montreal-based Stay22 secured a $122 million minority growth investment from Summit Partners in February. The startup uses AI to help publishers, creators and event organizers turn their audiences’ interest in travel into bookings and affiliate revenue.

Home-swapping platform Kindred announced an $85 million Series C led by Index Ventures in February. The San Francisco-based startup operates a members-only network where travelers exchange stays in one another’s homes. Its announcement also included a $40 million Series B co-led by New Enterprise Associates and Figma CEO Dylan Field, bringing the combined funding disclosed that day to $125 million.

Another large deal went to Paris-based Naboo, which announced a $70 million Series B in February led by Lightspeed Venture Partners with participation from Notion Capital, Isai and Ternel. The company uses AI to help businesses source venues, organize corporate events and manage related purchasing and payments.

Several travel startups have found buyers in 2026, including companies developing AI tools for planning and booking trips. Amadeus acquired corporate travel AI assistant SkyLink in February, while Expedia acquired AI trip-planning startup Layla in July. Both deals illustrate a trend of established travel companies buying startups to expand their AI capabilities.

Expedia also completed its acquisition of venture-backed Tiqets, a booking platform for museums, attractions and experiences, in February.

On the IPO side, a potentially prominent prospective exit fell through. Travel experiences platform Klook withdrew its planned U.S. offering in October after having filed last November.

Still, the downturn in startup funding and dearth of IPOs in the sector hasn’t affected one of the bigger now-public players in the space. Corporate travel booking and expense management platform Navan has seen its stock rise nearly 60% this year. Formerly called TripActions, it began trading on Nasdaq under NAVN in October 2025. Its stock closed at $27 on Oct. 28, up about 58% this year from its Dec. 31 closing price of $17.08. It was also 8% above its $25 IPO price, meaning much of this year’s gain recovered from losses following the listing.

#5441. Coinbase's October 26 Perpetual Conversion: The Crypto Index the CFTC Waiver Excludes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Coinbase wants six futures contracts to stop expiring on October 26. The CFTC letter it leans on covers five of them by design, and its own footnote points away from the sixth.

The Division of Market Oversight issued Letter 26-29 on October 3, 2026. The CFTC announced it two days later, on October 5, in Release 9308-26. Coverage then focused on the headline that exchanges can now strip expiry dates from perpetual-style index futures. The Merkle flagged the relief's hard October 20 stop on October 19, and outlets like Finance Magnates and FinanceFeeds ran the same window. That coverage, however, predates what Coinbase filed next. This breakdown sets the October 19 filing beside the letter's text, because the two don't line up cleanly.

Meanwhile, the CFTC is working on retail crypto leverage through a different door. As NullTX's earlier breakdown shows, the actual-delivery ANPRM (2026-20888) takes comments until December 14. Perpetuals on registered exchanges skip that process. Instead, they move through staff letters and self-certification.

Coinbase asked for the relief on October 1, and the Division granted it two days later. The letter says staff won't recommend enforcement if a DCM drops expiry dates from existing perpetual-style contracts, as long as the DCM meets eight conditions. First, it must gather feedback from holders of open positions. Next, it must give at least five calendar days' notice and let them close out under the old terms. It must also disclose the risks and change no other material term. Finally, it must file under the CFTC's rules, notify the Division and certify compliance.

Coinbase's Submission #2026-67 then names six contracts: US500, Tech100, Defense10, AI10, China10 and Coin50. It says everything except the expiry stays the same, and that the exchange knows of no substantive opposition. The contract list reached the CFTC by email on October 16.

Letter 26-29 defines its scope by asset class. A footnote shuts out any perpetual-style contract referencing something other than a broad-based security index. Coin50, by contrast, follows the Coinbase 50 Index, and Rule 1148 in the filing itself calls it a futures contract based on a cryptocurrency. In other words, the letter's scope and Coin50's own rule text point in opposite directions.

Crypto contracts did have their own relief. Letter 26-19, issued June 12 to Bitnomial and Coinbase Derivatives, covered digital commodities only and carried the same eight conditions. Even so, it says its positions expire on June 30, 2026. It rests on the Commission's May 29 order and its perpetuals policy statement.

Letter 26-29 sets October 20, 2026 as the day its no-action positions expire. It doesn't say whether implementation itself must happen by then, or only the notice and filing. Coinbase filed on October 19, one day early, but picked October 26 to go live. That choice matters. Ten business days from October 19 lands on November 2, and Coinbase specifically asked to skip that wait. As a result, going live on October 26 depends on the relief still applying.

Without relief, the Division's own words make the path clear. Letter 26-19 says certifications that remove expiry dates will generally draw a stay under Regulation 40.6(c). A stay then gives the Commission another 90 days to review and opens a 30-day public comment period.

Neither side has explained the gap. Searches of news coverage and official channels turned up no statement from Coinbase or the CFTC on whether Coin50 sits inside Letter 26-29, on what authority covers it after October 20, or on why the filing's October 26 date falls after the letter's expiry. We also found no CFTC stay notice and no extension or amendment of Letter 26-29. Likewise, the Coinbase posts we found cover other perpetual launches, not this conversion.

That silence doesn't mean a problem exists. Coinbase may be relying on authority the documents don't mention, and the CFTC may read the letter's dates differently than we do. Still, the paper trail shows a crypto-based contract sitting under relief written for stock indexes, with a start date that falls after that relief expires.

Three developments would settle it: a CFTC stay notice, a new or amended staff letter, or a clarification from Coinbase Derivatives.

Whichever arrives first tells us whether the first U.S.-listed crypto index perpetual goes live on schedule or lands in a 90-day review.

Prolonged moderation in the App Store, lasting more than a month and a half, has forced the onXRP team to adjust its original plans. Faced with bureaucratic delays on Apple’s side, Dutch entrepreneur Kaj Leroy (@BradPunkhouse) and his colleague Henk decided to launch their new product in a browser format.

Apparently, the release of a progressive web app (PWA) next week is intended to bypass the technical restrictions of mobile platforms and provide prompt access to a unique trading method for users of all devices, including Android and PC.

Based on Leroy’s public statements, the new product was not conceived as a direct competitor to existing decentralized exchanges or AMM pools on the XRP Ledger (XRPL). On the contrary, the platform is positioned as a complementary tool that supplements solutions already operating in the ecosystem.

The exact algorithms of the system are still being kept secret, but the key emphasis has shifted to integration with social platforms. The developer claims that the product will allow users to earn income from their usual activity on the social network X (Twitter), without having to make classic trades themselves.

@Iknowhim589 regardless, it really is unique there is nothing like it on the xrpl i think u will love it because u can earn with what u already do on x, without trading

It can be assumed that in this way the team expects to involve a broader internet audience in on-chain activity, monetizing their social attention and converting it into transaction volume for the entire blockchain.

In parallel, Leroy is actively developing the trading card game (TCG) sector, promoting the thesis that a global bull market has begun in this niche. His Fuzzycards project has already released about 100,000 digital booster packs on XRPL, which implement a mechanic of burning NFTs to receive real physical cards.

According to the entrepreneur, such a hybrid format today attracts a mass audience much more effectively than standard digital collections. To date, Leroy has not officially announced a direct connection between Fuzzycards and the upcoming web app.

Nevertheless, based on the general context of the ecosystem’s development, one can assume potential synergy in the future: a social earning tool on X technically looks like an effective add-on for attracting traffic and scaling gaming communities.

How justified these assumptions are will become clear after the release scheduled for next week.

#5437. Gemini Boss Slams Crypto-Hater Lagarde Following Her Resignation Announcement

Gemini co-founder Tyler Winklevoss took a jab at European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde after her unexpected resignation announcement.

"Your legacy will be to fight crypto and fail. Good luck in your next endeavor!" Winklevoss commented on Lagarde's resignation announcement on X.

Lagarde announced today that she will resign from her position on Feb. 7, 2027, which will be about nine months before her eight-year term is supposed to be over.

The ECB president, who has been at the helm of the ECB since November 2019, thanked her colleagues and those who have supported her over the past seven years.

It has been confirmed that the selection of her successor will be carried out by the European Council.

Lagarde has long been an outspoken critic of cryptocurrencies, especially Bitcoin.

Back in January 2021, she characterized Bitcoin as a very speculative asset. She also accused the cryptocurrency of enabling illicit financial operations.

During the Reuters Next conference, Lagarde said Bitcoin has been used for "funny business" and money laundering. Lagarde called for global coordination of regulations on cryptocurrencies.

The criticism further escalated when Lagarde said in May 2022 that cryptocurrencies are worth virtually nothing.

"My very humble assessment is that it is worth nothing," Lagarde said during an interview on Dutch television.

Lagarde stated that cryptocurrencies do not have underlying assets that would give investors a solid anchor of safety.

She also warned about inexperienced retail investors risking their savings in speculative crypto investments.

The ECB president also shared that one of her sons had made investments in cryptocurrencies despite her warnings.

In November 2023, she admitted that one of her sons had lost nearly all the money he invested in cryptocurrencies after he didn't heed her advice.

In January 2025, Lagarde emphatically ruled out the option of including Bitcoin in the reserves of European central banks.

Lagarde dismissed the proposal by Czech National Bank Governor Aleš Michl to study the possibility of investing in Bitcoin. According to Lagarde, the reserves need to be liquid, safe, and secure.

#5436. More Money, Fewer Checks: These 3 Charts Show The Divide Behind VC’s Record Funding Year

Startup capital is both more abundant than ever this year and yet scarcer. That contradiction has become increasingly visible in 2026 when analyzing Crunchbase data, and the trend continued through Q3.

Our data shows that despite record venture capital spending in 2026 — nearly $680 billion through Q3 — investors are writing fewer checks to seed and early-stage companies, the businesses one typically thinks of when we talk about startups.

One of the best ways to visualize this dichotomy is by looking at how much of the record global venture funding this year went to funding rounds across different tiers: less than $100 million, $100 million to just under $1 billion, and $1 billion and more.

As illustrated above, the funding surge this year is concentrated in those largest rounds, while the smaller-round market has essentially flatlined since 2023.

The massive surge in billion-dollar-plus rounds in Q1 and Q2, of course, was thanks to record-setting financings for OpenAI and Anthropic. But it’s not just those two companies concentrating capital at the top. About one-third of Q3 funding went to just 27 companies raising billion-dollar-plus rounds.

In North America, the largest startup market, deal counts have trended downward over several years, even as venture investment soared.

In Q3, reported deal counts in North America fell 16% year over year and 14% quarter over quarter, reaching the lowest quarterly total since 2023, even as North American funding dollars jumped 50% year over year to $92 billion. The contraction is concentrated in seed and early-stage deals — North American late-stage counts actually increased year over year.

Series B is a particularly stark illustration of the dollars-up-but-deals-down trend. Series B marks the stage when startups are maturing: they typically show some growth and traction but still have plenty of upside potential. But while dollars invested in U.S. startups at the Series B stage hit a multiyear high so far this year, deal count is on track to hit a multiyear low.

It’s a similar story among seed and Series A startups, with money concentrating into larger rounds even as deal count dips.

Anthropic, the biggest venture-backed private company of all, is slated to go public this month in a potential $2 trillion IPO, offering a prominent test of public investors’ appetite for the companies driving this venture boom.

A strong public-market reception could reinforce venture investors’ willingness to finance enormous AI bets, while a disappointing debut could put unicorn valuations under pressure.

But neither outcome guarantees that funding will reach a wider pool of startups. The real measure of a broader startup recovery we’ll be watching: whether deal counts start to rise alongside the dollars.

The large-scale rally was unexpectedly triggered by Elon Musk, namely his reaction to a tweet by Druckenmiller, which, no less unexpectedly, became the Wall Street legend's first-ever post on the former Twitter, now X, which Musk owns. The platform's owner quoted the post with the laconic word "Interesting."

In his debut post, Stanley Druckenmiller, who managed billion-dollar funds in the traditional market, announced that he had become an investor in the fintech startup trade[xyz]. The reason for the deal was the project's agreement with Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), the parent company of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE).

The partners intend to launch regulated round-the-clock (24/7) trading of perpetual futures contracts (perpetuals) in the U.S. Druckenmiller emphasized that, as an active market participant, he plans to personally use this product in his trading processes to optimize investment decisions.

The news instantly brought HYPE's daily trading volume to $796 million, lifting Hyperliquid's capitalization above $24.2 billion (9th place in the global ranking). The project fundamentally stands out with its Zero-VC model (without the participation of classic venture funds), where more than 76% of the supply is distributed to the community.

The synergy of entering the U.S. market through ICE, Druckenmiller's authority and Musk's attention allowed the asset to test peak price values with an FDV of $90.7 billion.

The founder of trade[xyz], under the pseudonym shadow, publicly responded to Musk's comment, proposing that the head of X combine onchain derivatives infrastructure with the algorithms of his AI company xAI. The developer stated that the emergence of strong AI (AGI) in capital markets is inevitable, and live trading will become its main benchmark.

According to shadow, a transparent distributed ledger in the style of Hyperliquid is the optimal mathematically secure environment for a superintelligent search for the fair price.

#5434. Sprout Ends at Block 3,543,405: What the ZIPs Say About ZEC in Orchard and Sapling

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Zcash has three older shielded pools, and only one of them has a shutdown date. On November 5, NU7 will make the 22,263 ZEC left in Sprout unspendable.

The 346,000 ZEC still in Orchard and the 420,000 ZEC in Sapling face no deadline at all.

But the Zcash specifications include one conditional warning that covers all three pools, and it has been widely misquoted. Let's go through the ZIPs to set out exactly what each document says about each pool, and what it doesn't.

Together, the three older pools hold about 788,000 ZEC. Any full node reports these balances directly through the valuePools field of its getblockchaininfo RPC, so anyone running a node can check them.

The three pools are on very different paths. Sprout has a fixed end. Orchard is closed to new deposits, but no spec sets a closing date. Sapling remains a supported pool.

Sprout's end has been planned for years. ZIP 211, written in 2019, stopped new value from entering Sprout. It described that as "a step toward being able to remove the Sprout shielded protocol."

ZIP 2003 takes the final step. It doesn't target Sprout directly. Instead, it bans an entire transaction format: from NU7 onward, "the transaction version number MUST be 5 or 6." Sprout transfers can only be written as version 4 transactions, so Sprout funds can no longer be spent.

ZIP 259, the NU7 deployment spec, sets the activation height at block 3,543,405 on mainnet. It states the result directly: "funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The wording matters. ZIP 2003 says it does not "unissue, burn, or otherwise make Sprout funds permanently unavailable." The coins stay counted in Zcash's issued supply, and the ZIP leaves open "the theoretical possibility of re-enabling v4 transactions, or of adding another facility to retrieve these funds." It also cautions that this "may never be re-enabled."

Recovering Sprout funds was already hard before the deadline. According to ZIP 2003, the retirement of zcashd just before NU6.3 "removed the only maintained software that still provided wallet functionality for Sprout." The pool has barely changed in the last few weeks: the widely reported figure of 22,309 ZEC has fallen only to 22,263, so about 46 ZEC has moved out since.

Orchard's situation is newer and more unusual. ZIP 258 activated NU6.3 at block 3,428,143 and sealed Orchard after a soundness vulnerability was found and fixed. Since then, the consensus rules have enforced three restrictions:

ZIP 229 explains why: Orchard held "a substantial portion of ZEC" when the vulnerability was fixed, so moving those funds to a fresh pool was meant to restore confidence in Zcash's total supply.

The migration has largely worked. ZecStats counts 3,278,499 ZEC moved out of Orchard, about 90.5% of what was in the pool at NU6.3. That leaves about 346,000 ZEC, roughly 2% of the circulating supply.

Sapling has the fewest restrictions of the three. Version 6 transactions support it as one of the "supported shielded pools," alongside Orchard and Ironwood, and none of the NU6.3 or NU7 ZIPs restricts it.

There's one catch for Sapling users that many people are missing. ZIP 259 says the version 4 ban covers "all version 4 transactions, including transparent-only and Sapling transactions, not only Sprout transfers." Sapling funds stay spendable after NU7, but only through version 5 or version 6 transactions. Wallets still building version 4 transactions need to switch before the upgrade. Pending or offline-signed version 4 transactions won't confirm afterward, and "re-signing alone cannot make a version 4 transaction valid."

The sentence behind the "inaccessible funds" headlines appears in ZIP 2005, "Ironwood Quantum Recoverability," and is repeated in ZIP 229:

"Recovery would not be possible for funds still in the Sprout, Sapling, or Orchard pools; all such funds would be inaccessible after their respective protocols are disabled."

The sentence before it explains the context. Zcash's existing shielded protocols depend on discrete logarithms being hard to compute. If an attacker, using a quantum computer or another method, could break that, the protocols might have to be disabled "to prevent such attacks." Only funds in Ironwood would be recoverable, through a recovery protocol designed to stay secure against quantum attacks.

So this is a contingency, not a schedule. It describes what would happen to funds in the older pools if a future cryptographic emergency forced Zcash to shut them down. No ZIP proposes doing that on any date. The practical advice behind it is plain: funds in Sprout, Sapling or Orchard "should be migrated to the Ironwood pool" to be covered by recovery.

The software is ready. The Zcash Foundation released Zebra 7.0.0 on October 22. Its changelog says it "supports the NU7 network upgrade on Mainnet, which activates at height 3,543,405." The release moves Zebra's database from format v28 to v29. Zebra 6.x can't read the new format, so the Foundation recommends backing up the old state first. The zcashd compatibility sidecar must also be updated to zebra-compat-v1.3.0. Earlier builds can't follow mainnet past NU7.

This upgrade carries more risk than usual. ZIP 259 waives Zcash's usual rule that old software must shut itself down before an upgrade. The spec warns that "operators of unsupported software may therefore remain online at activation and follow a pre-NU7 consensus branch."

For holders, the guidance from each pool's spec comes down to this:

On November 5, Sprout closes. The 766,000 ZEC in Sapling and Orchard face no deadline, but the specs still recommend moving it to Ironwood.

#5433. Bitcoin Settles Its $10.9 Billion Options Expiry Right on Max Pain After the Binance Hack

All reviews, research, news and assessments of any kind on The Tokenist are compiled using a strict editorial review process by our editorial team. Neither our writers nor our editors receive direct compensation of any kind to publish information on tokenist.com. Our company, Tokenist Media LLC, is community supported and may receive a small commission when you purchase products or services through links on our website. Click here for a full list of our partners and an in-depth explanation on how we get paid.

Bitcoin settled Friday’s $10.92 billion Deribit options expiry at $78,119, almost exactly on the $78,000 max pain level, after the $6.36 billion Binance hack knocked it from $80,850 to a $76,500 low overnight.

That low touched BTC’s 200-day EMA, the long-term trend line, to within $32. BTC trades at $77,620, down 3.2% in 24 hours, and the Fear & Greed Index fell from 51 to 30 in a day.

With about a third of Deribit’s open interest now gone, the options market is lighter than it has been all month. The next large date is November 27, when $3.55 billion expires with max pain at $80,000.

Coinbase Premium hit a 4-year low.The last time it was this low was in Nov 2022, right after the FTX collapse, when BTC bottomed.Market sentiment is bearish enough to be bullish, imo. pic.twitter.com/jab4bk1GIX

Discover: Bitcoin Braces for a $10.9 Billion Options Expiry With Max Pain at $78,000, Two Days After the Fed’s Split Hold: Can BTC Hold $79,000?

The drop came in two legs. BTC opened the 20:00 UTC hour on Thursday at $80,850 and hit $78,297 within minutes as news of the Binance breach spread, a 3.2% fall. It bounced, then slid again after 23:00 UTC and printed its $76,500 low just after 02:00 UTC on Friday, 5.4% below where the hour began.

Forced selling did much of the work. CoinGlass data showed $1.55 billion of crypto positions liquidated in 24 hours, 83.6% of them longs, with $501.6 million in BTC alone.

Smaller accounts bought the dip: the share of OKX accounts that are long jumped as the price fell, and open interest rose by about $210 million into the low. Funding on OKX’s BTC perpetual stayed positive throughout, so longs are still paying shorts.

Implied volatility told a more cautious story. Deribit’s DVOL index, which tracks the 30-day volatility options traders are pricing in, jumped from 37 before the hack to 42 just before midnight UTC and has only eased back to 38.7.

About 135,000 BTC of options expired on Deribit at 08:00 UTC on Friday, the last Friday of the month, when monthly contracts settle. Max pain, the strike where the most options expire worthless, sat at $78,000. Deribit settled the contracts at $78,119.01.

The book was heavily tilted toward calls. Deribit data reported before the expiry put the put/call ratio at 0.53, close to two calls for every put. With BTC settling just above $78,000, most of those calls, bets that BTC would be higher by the end of October, expired worthless.

Once the expiry cleared, Deribit’s BTC options open interest stood at 285,073 BTC, or about $22.1 billion, as of 11:17 UTC.

BTC options notional by Deribit expiry as of 11:17 UTC on October 30, 2026. Source: Deribit.

Max pain isn’t a forecast; BTC often settles far from it. But the November levels frame the range traders are betting on: puts clustered at $74,000 to $76,000, right around the 200-day EMA, and calls stacked from $90,000 up.

One more sign of caution: in the 24 hours to 11:17 UTC on Friday, Deribit traders bought 1.63 BTC of puts for every BTC of calls, the reverse of the call-heavy book that just expired.

On the daily chart since early August, BTC is back where it spent most of September: between its 200-day EMA at $76,468 and its 50-day EMA at $80,593. Friday’s low wick stopped $32 above the 200-day line, which BTC has closed above every day since its late-August breakout.

August 2 to October 30, 2026: BTCUSDT 1D chart. Source: Binance.

The levels line up with the options book:

BTC has tested this 200-day zone before. In mid-September, it dipped to $74,968, held, and ran to $87,395 within a week. Friday’s buyers are betting on the same bounce, as the OKX long/short ratio shows.

Discover: Bitcoin Swings Less Than Coinbase and Oracle, Yet Crypto Stocks Move Up to 2.4 Times as Hard: Why?

For Bitcoin, the next test is Binance itself. If withdrawals reopen smoothly within the promised 48 hours, the call-heavy positioning that just expired worthless could rebuild toward the $90,000 strikes. If they don’t, the puts at $74,000 to $76,000 are where traders have already placed their bets.

#5432. Polymarket Hit by Massive Hack

A massive security breach has reportedly seen nearly 1,000 accounts on the crypto-based prediction market Polymarket drained, with the attack leading to losses of more than $2.6M.

Blockchain analyst Conor Grogan revealed that a total of 995 accounts were hit by the attack, resulting in losses of roughly $2.65 million.

Polymarket has seen 995 accounts drained by a hacker, for $2,654,211.42. Largest losses were 341k and 307k Hacker has converted all funds to POL (most likely to avoid freezing) https://t.co/PjT2QhgBSa

The two biggest losses detected by Grogan were $341K and $307K.

Moreover, the analyst also revealed that the attacker has converted all stolen funds into Polygon's native token (POL). This move might have been made to avoid having the funds frozen.

"If you are a @Polymarket user lock your account. I just got drained $800,000," a trader warned via X.

The trader also claimed that a friend lost another $600K and warned users not to interact with the website.

As noted by blockchain investigator StarPlatinum, the attacker stole roughly $2.68M in just one hour.

The data shows that at about 17:05 UTC, an empty wallet began receiving funds.

At 17:25 UTC, the wallet had amassed roughly $412K.

However, the figure jumped to $2.02M at 17:50 UTC and reached roughly $2.68M at 18:05 UTC.

In total, the attacker has amassed some 28.6M POL tokens, as noted.

So far, it appears that the attack might have occurred due to a hack of a third-party JavaScript component that was embedded in the Polymarket website.

It's not the first time that the popular prediction market has faced a massive hack leading to a multimillion-dollar security breach.

We've identified & fixed an issue impacting our international platform, Polymarket⁠.com. One of our 3rd party providers was compromised, and we have referred this to relevant law enforcement. Anyone who has been impacted will be made whole. Out of an abundance of caution, we have temporarily halted trading & are working to bring the platform back online.

In June, Polymarket also faced a similar hack. The attack happened when hackers compromised a third-party vendor and injected malicious JavaScript into the frontend of Polymarket.

In total, some $2.94 million was stolen from at least 11 wallets.

Now, Polymarket has reportedly confirmed that the security breach occurred due to a hack of a third-party service provider.

The company also vowed to make every affected user whole. In other words, users who suffered losses due to the attack will be compensated.

#5431. China’s Largest Startup Deal Ever Lifts Global Venture Funding To $59B In October

Global venture funding in October totaled $59 billion, a 45% jump from a year earlier, per Crunchbase data, in large part due to a record-setting deal for China’s DeepSeek. The company’s $15.9 billion funding round marked the largest-ever venture deal for a Chinese company ever, and came in the same month that two other frontier labs raised blockbuster Series A rounds totaling at or close to $1 billion.

The bulk of October’s venture funding was invested in the two leading countries for startup investment, with companies based in the U.S. and China raising $28 billion and $20.6 billion last month, respectively. The last time more than $20 billion was invested in China in a single month was June 2018, when Ant Group raised $14 billion in its Series C funding.

Funding concentrated in seven companies that raised billion-dollar rounds, accounting for just over 40% of October’s venture funding. These large amounts were invested in frontier labs, manufacturing, energy, semiconductors, prediction markets and spend management software. Private equity led much of this funding, along with a few multistage venture firms including Sequoia Capital, Index Ventures and Lux Capital.

DeepSeek’s $15.9 billion raise at a valuation of $90 billion marked the largest private funding by a Chinese tech company on record. The deal places DeepSeek among the Top 10 most highly funded private companies. It also makes it the second most highly valued Chinese company after ByteDance, and the third most highly valued private frontier lab after U.S. companies Anthropic and OpenAI.

DeepSeek wasn’t the only Chinese frontier lab to raise big in October. Moonshot AI, a rival open-source lab, reportedly reached a $50 billion value in October, making it the 11th most valuable private company on The Crunchbase Unicorn Board. The startup has also reportedly confidentially filed to go public on the Hong Kong stock exchange.

Massachusetts-based manufacturing startup Re:Build raised the second-largest funding deal last month, a $2.1 billion round. The company partners with industrial companies and innovators from the product design phase to large-scale production and says it has 2.4 million square feet of manufacturing capacity.

Other large rounds last month went to Axiom, which raised $2 billion for power and grid capacity build out for data centers; spend-management platform Ramp, which raised $1.85 billion and said its ARR has reached $2 billion; open-source semiconductor company Tenstorrent, which says it  raised a $1.5 billion Series E funding and recently moved its  headquarters to Silicon Valley from Canada; prediction market Kalshi, which raised a $1 billion Series E; and frontier lab Flapping Airplanes, which raised a $1 billion Series A.

A further eight companies raised rounds north of $500 million last month. They spanned industries ranging from frontier labs, robotics, legal and chips, to agentic AI and healthcare. Among the most notable was TypeSafe AI, which says it raised an $870 million Series A funding on the heels of rapid developer adoption of its decision model Jev.

A total of 66% of global funding was in AI-driven companies in October, with semiconductor companies gaining market share this past month.

The U.S. IPO market was slow in anticipation of Anthropic’s November IPO. The offering could surpass even SpaceX’s record-setting June listing that raised $85.7 billion.

On the M&A front, at least nine venture-backed companies were acquired for more than $1 billion last month, including Uber’s acquisition of 19-year-old ezCater for $2.3 billion.

With two months remaining, 2026 has already set records for acquisitions, IPOs and funding rounds across major venture markets. October extended that momentum, but also highlighted how concentrated this cycle has become: Seven companies accounted for more than 40% of global funding, while AI-driven businesses captured two-thirds.

The question heading into year-end is how widely that momentum will spread, as Anthropic prepares to list in what could be the largest IPO of all time.

The data contained in this report comes directly from Crunchbase, and is based on reported data. Data is as of Nov. 2, 2026.

Cohere is targeting a $5 billion funding that was announced in October, without reporting an initial or final close. This funding was not included in the October monthly totals.

Note that data lags are most pronounced at the earliest stages of venture activity, with seed funding amounts increasing significantly after the end of a quarter/year.

Please note that all funding values are given in U.S. dollars unless otherwise noted. Crunchbase converts foreign currencies to U.S. dollars at the prevailing spot rate from the date funding rounds, acquisitions, IPOs and other financial events are reported. Even if those events were added to Crunchbase long after the event was announced, foreign currency transactions are converted at the historic spot price.

Seed and angel consists of seed, pre-seed and angel rounds. Crunchbase also includes venture rounds of unknown series, equity crowdfunding and convertible notes at $3 million (USD or as-converted USD equivalent) or less.

Early-stage consists of Series A and Series B rounds, as well as other round types. Crunchbase includes venture rounds of unknown series, corporate venture and other rounds above $3 million, and those less than or equal to $15 million.

Late-stage consists of Series C, Series D, Series E and later-lettered venture rounds following the “Series [Letter]” naming convention. Also included are venture rounds of unknown series, corporate venture and other rounds above $15 million. Corporate rounds are only included if a company has raised an equity funding at seed through a venture series funding round.

Technology growth is a private-equity round raised by a company that has previously raised a “venture” round. (So basically, any round from the previously defined stages.)

#5430. Hackers Target Crypto Users With Fake ChatGPT and Claude Apps

Cybercriminals have been using the hype surrounding artificial intelligence (AI) technologies to distribute cryptocurrency mining malware through fake desktop apps that mimic popular AI tools like ChatGPT and Claude.

In a recent report, cybersecurity vendor Check Point Research (CPR) said threat actors have been setting up fake GitHub repositories to advertise fake AI apps like GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus, among others.

The hackers have even set up dedicated GitHub.io sites that promote their fake AI apps and trick victims into downloading malicious files.

According to the CPR researchers, the attackers are using search engine optimization (SEO) manipulation to get their malicious sites to rank high on Google.

One of the most worrisome aspects of the campaign is how the attackers use legitimate software components from OpenAI and Anthropic to mask malicious activity.

The malicious ZIP archives that victims can download feature legitimate digitally signed executable files. These legitimate executables are bundled with malicious DLLs.

Once victims run the seemingly legitimate application, the malicious DLL gets loaded without their knowledge, thanks to the DLL sideloading technique.

This makes it very hard for victims to spot the attack since the malware relies on legitimate software to run its code.

At the end of the day, the attack leads to the installation of XMRig, a cryptocurrency miner that quietly uses the victims' resources to mine digital assets for the attackers.

Interestingly, the malware can also stop mining whenever it senses user activity so that it can evade detection.

In addition, CPR researchers discovered that the malware includes several techniques to make security investigations harder.

For example, it can pause execution for a very long time if it senses that it is not running under the expected executable file.

It also checks the keyboard language setting on a computer before going ahead with the infection.

The first GitHub repository for the campaign showed up in July 2026, and malicious downloads started popping up at the end of August.

At the moment, the payload is a cryptocurrency miner, but researchers have warned that YobaLoader can potentially be used to deploy other types of malware.

#5429. CoinDepo Revises Earn Rates to Reflect Asset Economics and Deployment Horizons

Neither our writers nor our editors receive direct compensation of any kind to publish information on tokenist.com. Our company, Tokenist Media LLC, is community supported and may receive a small commission when you purchase products or services through links on our website. Click here for a full list of our partners and an in-depth explanation on how we get paid.

CoinDepo is introducing revised Earn rates effective November 8, 2026. The changes connect the economics of each supported asset with the practical requirements of managing client capital across different account lengths.

Client deposits are placed into a diversified portfolio whose primary focus is lending. At the close of the second quarter of 2026, overcollateralized crypto lending represented 37% of deployed capital and microcredit programs represented 24%. Remaining allocations covered liquidity pools, real-world and private-market investments, stablecoin yield strategies, and market-neutral trading.

Income produced by these activities funds the interest paid to users and also covers operating costs and liquidity needs. The resulting APRs therefore align with the broader economics of operating the CoinDepo platform.

Daily APRs will decline for every asset listed in CoinDepo’s 30-asset update table. EURC is handled separately and keeps its 10% Daily APR. USDT and USDC Daily APRs will adjust from 17% to 15% while their Annual APRs change from 23% to 22%. BTC and ETH Daily APRs move from 12% to 11%, with Annual APR remaining at 18%.

Across the 30 assets, the difference between Daily and Annual rates expands from six percentage points to seven. The adjustments will also be asset-specific as well as period-specific; the Annual APR for Filecoin (FIL), for instance, will be changed from 18% to 12%.

Short-term funds require the platform to retain greater flexibility so that withdrawals can be met without delay. A more predictable funding horizon simplifies the planning of capital allocation and the matching of funds with available lending and investment opportunities. The wider gap between Daily and Annual APRs places greater weight on that planning advantage. Daily accounts continue to be offered for users who place priority on ready access to their funds.

CoinDepo’s open Monthly, Quarterly, Semi-Annual and Annual Interest Accounts will keep their current APR through the remainder of the active term. Revised rates apply only to accounts that are newly opened or renewed after the effective date. The complete before-and-after comparison appears in the platform’s Earn rate update, together with the business disclosures that describe the activities supporting client interest.

CoinDepo is a centralized digital asset platform that provides crypto interest accounts and portfolio-backed borrowing services.

#5428. Massive $5.9 Billion Binance Hack Hits XRP, BTC, ETH and Other Tokens

Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, has been hit with a massive security breach. Blockchain analysts believe the hackers have stolen nearly $6 billion in crypto from wallets linked to the exchange.

According to blockchain analytics firm Glassnode, the suspected hack initially involved crypto worth $5.3 billion.

The hackers made some of the biggest transfers out of the crypto exchange, including an estimated $1.66 billion in Tether (USDT), 17,985 Bitcoin (BTC) worth about $1.45 billion, and $767 million in USD Coin (USDC).

Other crypto tokens involved in the suspected hack included Ethereum (ETH), XRP, Solana (SOL), and Tron (TRX).

According to Glassnode, the suspicious outflows occurred sequentially across various blockchains. XRP transfers came first, followed by SOL, BTC, and others.

Glassnode also noted that the exchange's BNB balance wasn't touched.

The total suspicious outflows are close to $5.9 billion.

The total losses aren't known yet. Analysts are sharing different estimates as they watch funds jump from one blockchain address to another.

Changpeng Zhao (CZ), Binance's co-founder and former CEO, acknowledged the apparent security breach. At the same time, he assured Binance's customers that they are safe.

"It does look like a hack on Binance," Zhao wrote on X.

User funds are safe! It does look like a hack on Binance. Appreciate the quick freeze from Tether (~$971m) and Circle (~$823m). I don't manage Binance (.com) anymore, but as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.

The billionaire commended the quick response of stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle, which froze about $971 million and $823 million, respectively.

"I'm not running Binance (.com) anymore, but as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered," Zhao emphasized.

In his next post, Zhao admitted that the actual losses could be higher, even though an analyst estimated that about $1B in exposure remained after the assets were frozen. But he again reaffirmed that the losses would be covered.

The quick response from major stablecoin issuers was crucial.

Tether's CEO Paolo Ardoino revealed that the company had frozen over 1.567 billion USDT linked to the potential hack at Binance.

"Protecting the industry and our partners is our main priority," Ardoino stated.

Meanwhile, Circle's CEO Jeremy Allaire confirmed that the company had frozen over $800M in USDC in coordination with law enforcement.

Later on, Binance provided an update. The exchange confirmed that the total amount of frozen assets came to $2.54B. Binance also warned that this number could increase as the investigation is ongoing.

If the highest estimates of stolen funds are accurate, the Binance incident could be the biggest crypto hack ever.

In February 2025, the record was set when crypto exchange Bybit lost about $1.5 billion worth of Ethereum in an attack that was linked to North Korean hackers.

Following the suspected breach at Binance, the broader crypto market fell.

Bitcoin briefly dipped below $79,000. Ethereum fell below $2,300. XRP is down by almost 7%. Binance's native crypto token BNB dropped even harder. It dipped about 7% during the initial response.

Zcash is preparing to triple transaction speed as its NU7 network upgrade approaches November 5, but governance tensions and falling prices are testing investor confidence.

The Zcash upgrade will reduce target block times from 75 seconds to 25 seconds, making transaction confirmations significantly faster. The activation is planned for block height 3,543,405, according to the network’s deployment schedule.

Zcash Network Upgrade 7 mainnet activation height is being set for Block 3,543,405 (~November 5th 2026) pic.twitter.com/C4D5Dch61l

The technical changes arrive as Zcash faces a separate debate over its community-grants funding system. ZEC has also suffered recent price weakness, leaving traders weighing network improvements against growing uncertainty over its future direction.

The upcoming Zcash upgrade introduces several changes beyond faster block production. Under ZIP 218, the network will target a new block every 25 seconds, down from 75 seconds. That could reduce the waiting time for three transaction confirmations from nearly four minutes to around 75 seconds.

The upgrade also introduces limits on shielded transaction activity, designed to improve network efficiency and protect wallets against spam.

Meanwhile, ZIP 235 will remove 60% of transaction fees from circulation and place them into a reserve. The mechanism is intended to support future mining rewards as block subsidies decline.

Node operators must also upgrade their software to remain on the network’s consensus chain. at present, Zcash Foundation has released Zebra 7.0.0, which supports NU7 on mainnet and includes additional synchronization and security improvements.

The Zcash Upgrade comes as the project faces renewed debate over how its development ecosystem should be funded. Zcash co-founder Sean Bowe recently proposed ending the automatic allocation of 8% of newly issued ZEC to the Zcash Community Grants program.

Bowe said that the program already holds approximately $125 million after existing commitments, enough to fund years of development without continuing automatic inflows.

His proposal would redirect the allocation toward a reserve supporting future mining rewards. The committee would retain its existing funds and continue distributing grants.

The proposal does not directly cite that controversy, instead focusing on the size of the grants treasury and long-term funding sustainability.

ZEC has also faced selling pressure ahead of the upgrade. Recent market coverage placed the token near $1,135 after an approximately 11% decline, highlighting the disconnect between improving network fundamentals and short-term price performance.

MetaMask is facing fresh questions about its future after Consensys launched a new institutional settlement network targeting banks, asset managers and financial market infrastructure providers.

The announcement puts Consensys’ institutional ambitions in the spotlight just weeks before its planned separation from MetaMask. The move could also leave the popular wallet competing independently while its former parent pursues Wall Street.

Introducing Sovereign Network Interoperability by Consensys.State-of-the-art interoperability that enables institutions to do business freely, settling securities, exchanging currencies and posting collateral across ledgers, without bridges or moving assets onto a shared…

Consensys unveiled Sovereign Network Interoperability at Devcon, introducing infrastructure designed to coordinate transactions across independently operated financial networks. Can MetaMask maintain its position as institutional blockchain adoption accelerates?

The new Sovereign Network Interoperability platform aims to help institutions settle securities, exchange currencies, and move collateral across separate blockchain networks.

Its bridgeless design keeps assets on their original ledgers while coordinating transactions between approved counterparties. Consensys says the system uses cryptographic verification to reduce reliance on additional trusted intermediaries.

The platform targets four major financial workflows, including securities settlement, wholesale payments, collateral mobility, and tokenized fund transactions.

Consensys plans to support Ethereum-compatible networks and protocols such as the Ethereum Economic Zone and Inter-Blockchain Communication. Canton connectivity is also planned.

The launch builds on Consensys’ existing institutional infrastructure, including Linea, Hyperledger Besu and Teku. The company is positioning itself as a technology provider for financial institutions seeking private, always-on blockchain settlement.
